title: Jerusalem Humbled, Then Rescued
overview: Isaiah warns that Jerusalem, going through the motions of religion while scheming in secret, will be brought to the brink by a siege, then suddenly rescued, and finally renewed so that the blind see and the oppressed rejoice.

parts.label: Ariel under siege (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Ariel is a name for Jerusalem, David's city; its exact meaning is uncertain, but it may mean "altar hearth" (the place where sacrifices burned), hinting the city itself will become a scene of fire. The people keep their yearly festivals, yet the LORD says he himself will surround the city through its enemies, until its proud voice is reduced to a faint whisper from the dust, like the eerie voices mediums claimed to raise from the dead.

parts.label: Enemies vanish like a dream (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: In a sudden reversal, the attacking armies are scattered like dust and chaff, their hopes of taking the city as empty as a hungry person's dream of food. Many readers connect this with the Assyrian army that besieged Jerusalem in Isaiah's day and then abruptly withdrew (Isaiah 37).

parts.label: Blind and a sealed scroll (vv. 9-12)
parts.note: The people are pictured as stunned and staggering, as if drunk, unable to take in God's message. It has become like a sealed scroll: the educated say they can't open it, and those who can't read say they can't read it, so no one grasps it.

parts.label: Lip service and secret plans (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: God objects to worship that is words and learned routine while the heart is elsewhere, and warns that the clever advisers' wisdom will fail; Jesus later quoted verse 13 against empty religion. The secret plans likely refer to leaders quietly seeking an alliance with Egypt against Assyria, acting as if the clay could tell the potter he knows nothing.

parts.label: Everything turned around (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: The forests of Lebanon becoming farmland is a picture of a world remade, where the deaf hear the very scroll that had been sealed and the blind see. The humble and poor rejoice because the bullies, mockers and people who twist the courts with false testimony are gone; city courts met at the town gate.

parts.label: Jacob no longer ashamed (vv. 22-24)
parts.note: Jacob, the ancestor of Israel, is pictured as no longer going pale with shame over his descendants, because they now honor God as holy. Even the confused and the grumblers come to understand and accept teaching.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the closing promise of renewal (vv. 17-24) mainly described Judah's recovery after the Assyrian crisis, is fulfilled in Jesus and the church, or still awaits a future restoration of Israel.
think: Is there something you keep doing out of habit even though your heart is no longer in it, and what keeps you doing it?
